items.title: Why agent swarms get better at optimizing code as they grow
items.story_key: story|title:why agent swarms get better at optimizing code as they grow
items.content_excerpt: Vaibhav Kumar / Ibrahim Sheikh / Peter Zhong / Saurav Joshi / Patrick Ma / Jason Dellaluce / Darsh Patel / Phil MacEachron / Michele Catasta · Nov 19, 2026 Fred Brooks observed in 1975 that adding programmers to a late project makes it later because every new engineer brings more coordination than work. Early research on agent swarms found that multi-agent systems often trailed a single agent once coordination costs were accounted for [1–4]. We tested whether this still holds for today’s models using performance engineering tasks to examine how scaling inference-time compute drives both speedups and emergent coordination mechanics. On NumPy, one Claude Opus 5.5 agent made the workloads 3.7× faster in two hours, while a swarm of 32 Opus agents, given the same two hours, reached 18.9×. GPT-6.2 Astra was the strongest solo agent we tested, yet its swarms got worse as they grew. Given no instructions on how to organize, each model’s swarms arranged themselves differently, and the differences mattered. The best swarms sent few direct messages; workers claimed tasks and shared results on a common board. The ones that struggled routed everything through the coordinator, whose inbox grew with every agent added. The other deciding factor was the shape of the work. While codebases with independent problems allowed each new agent to contribute usefully, highly constrained tasks often led extra agents to compete for the same code. On Replit, an agent swarm works much like an engineering team. Each agent, coordinator or worker, is a full Replit Agent with its own cloud sandbox, so it can build, run, and profile code without getting in anyone else’s way. Agents share a repository rather than a filesystem, and their work comes together through branches and pushes. They also share context through three communication channels: a swarm board that lets agents open threads, reply, address posts to specific teammates, and set their status; direct messaging between teammates; and transcripts that let agents read what a teammate tried and why without interrupting it. Agent Habitat provides the elastic compute behind this. Each sandbox is an isolated Linux microVM whose CPU, memory, and disk grow with the workload, so a coordinator can start hundreds of workers quickly, and a single agent can work across several sandboxes at once. items.title: Show HN: Git blame for AI code, down to the agent session
items.story_key: story|title:git blame for ai code down to the agent session
items.content_excerpt: git blame stops at a commit and a name, usually yours. KeepPlain follows the line to the Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Pi or Antigravity session behind it and opens the turn: what you asked, what the agent tried first, why it changed. Free for personal use. Say yes when keepplain enable asks about git hooks: they add the session’s id to your commits, and blame follows it. Ask your agent about a line, and it follows git to the session that made the change, reads the turns from your request to the commit, and answers with quotes. It says which turns it read and how the session was found. When a prompt asks where code came from, the plugin adds one line to it: git shows what changed, the session the change was made in shows why. So the agent runs git log or git blame first, then asks KeepPlain for the session by the commit, its trailer, its subject and the files. The match is made on your computer; the prompt goes nowhere. git blame shows the last commit. In your team’s search, a GitHub link ending in #L42 becomes the line’s history: the commit that added it, every commit that changed it, and the sessions behind each one. Switch it on for your team and the GitHub App keeps one comment on each pull request, updated as commits change: which commits came from a session, which were agent-assisted, and the session behind each. Sessions behind this pull request. The commits that came from an agent session or with an agent’s help. No new version control and no IDE extension. The agent you already use runs git, then asks KeepPlain. git blame names only the last commit. Your agent asks git for every commit that touched the line, up to eight. One trailer line in the commit message, written by KeepPlain’s prepare-commit-msg hook when a commit holds a session’s work. Only the id travels with your push. The session doesn’t. By the commit, the trailer, the subject and the files, across your sessions from all five agents, and your team’s. From your request to the change: the reasoning and your decision, not the whole log. The request is your last real one before the change; a “yes” or “continue” is skipped. The answer above: what happened, your words, the commit, and which turns it came from. If the session was found another way, by its edits or not at all, the answer says that too. The commit says which session it came from. The answer quotes that session and the turns it read. items.title: How to build a knowledge factory for AI agents
items.summary: The knowledge factory is how LangChain keeps its agents' company knowledge current: agents flag what's missing, and a curator agent fixes it in the background.
items.story_key: story|title:how to build a knowledge factory for ai agents
items.content_excerpt: In order to make AI work for your company, the missing bit is not better models, it’s not just more context - it’s better knowledge. It’s knowledge of how your company works, what standards for operating you have in place, where data is stored and how it’s accessed. Your most efficient employees have this knowledge in their head. They know who to talk to, where to go to answer questions, why you do things in a particular way. That knowledge is often tacit, implicit, scattered - sometimes present only in their head, sometimes scattered across a variety of documents. In order to make AI work for your company, you need to collect, curate, and maintain a representation of that knowledge to pass to agents. The system that helps you do that is what we’re calling a knowledge factory. We’ve built this at LangChain in a few ways. Our internal GTM and content studio agents are powered by a knowledge factory. LangSmith Engine (our agent that runs over traces and suggests fixes) maintains a knowledge factory per agent as well. This blog shares our learnings. Knowledge is the reusable understanding we maintain so it can do that task correctly: what a metric means, which source to trust, or how we handle a particular situation. Sometimes written down, often not. A knowledge factory turns scattered documents and experience into knowledge that can become context for future work. So knowledge is a form of context that the agent will get, but it’s often not (and shouldn’t be) the only context the agent gets. Other types of context you already ingest/store reliably, and that can just be provided directly to the agent (see the section on quickly changing data below). The idea of software factories has risen sharply over the past year and a half. The idea is that rather than having your best engineers actually build software, they should build the factory (the systems) to help everyone at the company build software more efficiently. The actual building of the software can be done by agents. General knowledge work is now following a similar path. Agents are good enough to make presentations, launch videos, do outbound. You should be leveraging them as much as possible for those tasks. But in order for them to accomplish those tasks they need all that tacit, implicit, scattered knowledge. That is where you should devote resources. You need to build that knowledge, and more importantly a factory to collect, curate and maintain that knowledge. That is what will let you outsource m

items.title: Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup
items.story_key: story|variant:mini|title:welcome inkling 2 mini cutting edge performance for your local setup
items.content_excerpt: TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost. Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release! We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware. This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones. Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384. The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights. Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages . Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed. Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate

items.title: LangSmith Tool Gateway: Secure, governed tool use for agents
items.summary: LangSmith Tool Gateway, now in Public Beta, handles credentials, identity, and access for every agent tool call, with policies, approvals, and traces.
items.story_key: story|title:langsmith tool gateway secure governed tool use for agents
items.content_excerpt: Agents are moving beyond the chat window to take on more proactive and ambient work. Instead of waiting for a prompt, they run on a schedule or are triggered by events, and they’re handling longer tasks without someone checking every step. That makes them much more useful, but it also means teams need to control which tools each agent can call and whose identity it acts with, and keep a record of every action it takes. Today, we’re launching LangSmith Tool Gateway in Public Beta, on the LangSmith Agent Platform . Tool Gateway is a managed tool layer that handles credentials, identity, and access for every agent tool call, making it simple to govern the actions your agents take. Tool Gateway makes it easier and faster for engineering teams to grant agents access to new tools in a controlled manner and without hand-rolling auth each time. Security and compliance teams can use LangSmith to trace and audit tool calls as part of agent monitoring. The two-minute video below shows how Tool Gateway controls which tools each agent can call and whose identity it acts with. When agents are in production, platform teams need visibility into what each agent did, controls over which tools and models it can use, and usage policies that limit spend and risk. With LangSmith, developers can build, run, and improve agents in a single platform. LLM Gateway governs the model calls agents make. With it, you can set spend limits and model fallbacks, add rate limits, redact personal data and secrets, and provides visibility within the agent trace with rich information on model calls such as latency, fallbacks, failures, guardrails triggered, etc. Tool Gateway lives in LangSmith alongside LLM Gateway, and provides governance across this lifecycle. Tool Gateway simplifies tool lists for agents, implementing policies on usage, managing identity for tool use, and as with LLM Gateway, provides visibility within the agent trace through rich information on tool calls such as servers, users, outcomes, latency, etc. Together, Tool Gateway and LLM Gateway provide comprehensive visibility and governance over agent actions and spend. Agents in production need to serve hundreds or thousands of users, each with their own set of permissions. This means managing and refreshing a large volume of tokens, and carefully managing and recording access for security and audit requirements. items.title: Evaluating safeguarding in multi-turn conversations with AI assistants
items.summary: Conversational AI assistants are now used for personal and emotional support. Developers report improvements in how new models respond to sensitive conversations, yet users and civil society continue to raise concerns about their behaviour in real-world, repeated interactions that safety evaluations rarely capture. Often, evaluations present signs of distress clearly and in a single message, even though people may reveal their struggles gradually in otherwise ordinary conversations. We worked with three community mental health support workers to test if models provide the same level of safeguarding when cues are shared all at once or gradually over time. We designed nine scenarios in which a user shares cues related to depression, psychosis, or domestic abuse. For each scenario, the support workers established a gold standard response, ranging from signposting support to pausing the everyday task to address safeguarding. We presented five cues either together in one message or dispersed across a conversation. Across more than 7,400 conversations, we evaluated six widely used models from five developers. GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4, and Llama 4 Maverick met the support workers' standards in just 26-59% of conversations when cues were concentrated, and only 3-6% when dispersed. Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 showed a smaller gap, meeting the standards in 68-97% of concentrated conversations and 59-87% of dispersed conversations. Even the best-performing model, Claude Opus 5, fell short of the gold standard in 13% of conversations when cues were dispersed. Safety evaluations centred on explicit, legible concerns can overstate how well safeguards protect people when signs of distress emerge gradually or indirectly through ordinary conversations. For claims of improved safety to be taken seriously, developers must design and assess safeguards around how people actually communicate.

items.title: Harnessing Medical Visual-Language Models with Agentic Evidence Management
items.summary: Medical vision-language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. But do these agents use the resulting evidence effectively? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these properties. We therefore construct Mask-Evidence MedVQA, a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four image types, where each question is paired with an answer-relevant ground-truth mask and multiple possible renderings. Our study reveals two limitations of direct tool use. First, evidence presentation matters. Different renderings of the same fixed mask can substantially change model behavior. Second, masks introduce an evidence trade-off. Highlighting a relevant region can expose diagnostic evidence the model previously missed, but the added visual cue can also induce incorrect associations. As a result, even a ground-truth mask can correct some answers while turning initially correct ones into incorrect ones. Together, these findings show that acquiring the right mask is not enough. An agent must also decide how to present the evidence and whether it should change the answer. We therefore introduce TUNE (Tool Use is Not Enough), an evidence-management harness that explicitly manages what evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. Across three public medical VQA benchmarks, evidence management improves the fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone's mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. Full TUNE improves over direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks and achieves competitive results against existing medical VLMs and agents.

items.title: Your Software Factory Needs a Bill of Materials | Daniel Meppiel
items.summary:
Developers are about to write skills instead of code, and Microsoft's Daniel Meppiel argues the software factory that runs them needs versioning, a bill of materials and signed receipts before enterprises will trust it.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:
https://tessl.co/7jw

Then stay for Daniel's full DevCon talk, Version Your Factory, Not Just Your Code, on agent contracts, signed receipts and the evidence a regulated enterprise needs before it auto-merges.

– Why developers will write skills and prose instead of code

items.title: Inkling 2 Mini on vLLM: Day-0 Support for a Looped Model
items.summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini from day 0: a looped MoE that runs its middle layers three times, with per-pass KV caches, gated messages between passes, fused kernels and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|variant:mini|title:inkling 2 mini on vllm day 0 support for a looped model
items.content_excerpt: Thinking Machines announced Inkling 2 Mini today. vLLM supports it and its variable-loop research checkpoint, TML-d24-varloop-research , on day 0 on NVIDIA Blackwell, Hopper and DGX Spark. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped model: its middle 12 layers run three times per token with shared weights, each pass with its own KV cache and gated messages from the pass before. It is a multimodal MoE with 26B total and 3.5B active parameters, up to 1M tokens of context and a native DSpark speculator. We provide a Docker image with Inkling 2 Mini support, vllm/vllm-openai:inkling-2-mini . You can serve the model with: And the variable-loop research checkpoint, here with 2 passes and one KV cache shared across passes: Figure 1. The prelude and coda run once; the loop core runs three passes, each reading messages from the one before. Prelude, core, coda. The 24 layers split into a prelude (layers 0–5), a loop core (layers 6–17) and a coda (layers 18–23). The prelude and coda run once each; the core runs three passes with shared weights, and the coda continues from the last pass. Each group of six layers is one block of the block attention residuals used in Inkling 2 Small, so one pass of the core produces exactly two blocks. Every pass starts from the prelude's output. A plain looped model feeds pass p's output into pass p + 1. Here, all three passes start from that same output, and pass p + 1 sees pass p only through messages. Messages are read at every sublayer. From the second pass on, each core sublayer input (the attention's query, key and value inputs and the MLP input) gets its own message, read from the previous pass's two blocks by an attention-residual read with a learned query per layer and input type. A rank-64 controller then merges the message into the input, per channel: With 12 core layers and 4 inputs each, every later pass reads 48 messages per token. Because the query, key and value inputs get different messages, the sliding-window layers, which project all three from one input in the first pass, take three separate inputs in later passes. Each pass keeps its own memory. Every core layer has a KV cache and a conv-state cache per pass, so pass p attends to the keys and values that pass p computed for earlier tokens. The model has 24 layers but 48 KV caches and 48 conv-state caches. DSpark draft from inside the loop. items.title: Complete-SVD: A Functional Norm Approach to Low-Rank LLM Compression
items.summary: Post-training low-rank compression of neural networks must not only approximate the original weights but also preserve the model's input-output behavior. Recent output-aware methods measure the compression error beyond the compressed layer, at the model output, weighting logit changes by the observed next token or by the model's predicted probabilities. We propose Complete-SVD, a method for large language models that minimizes the $L_2$ distance between the logits of the original and compressed models, weighting all logit changes equally. Linearizing the network around the original weights, together with a Kronecker-factored approximation, reduces this objective to a weighted SVD with a closed-form solution. Its output-side factor is intractable to compute; we estimate it without bias from random probes, at a cost of $K$ backward passes per sequence, independent of vocabulary size and sequence length. At matched settings with uniform ranks and WikiText-2 calibration, Complete-SVD achieves the lowest C4 and PTB perplexity in every setting, and at ratio 0.7 under LEMS rank allocation. Replacing the $L_2$ distance by the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL-SVD), with the same estimation framework, lowers calibration perplexity in most settings and raises downstream accuracy, but raises cross-corpus perplexity. Complete-SVD also improves IFEval instruction-following accuracy over the strongest prior output-aware methods throughout.

  • Added support for naming a session's billing group with the attributionProject setting, for Claude apps gateways that set admin.billing_group_tag
  • Added /tui classic as the name for the non-fullscreen renderer; /tui default still works
  • Remote Control: Fixed stopping the server in worktree mode deleting a running session's git-ignored files, such as .env
  • Fixed self-hosted runners with --use-anthropic-git-proxy deleting a non-empty directory named by GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL at startup: the runner now keeps it, ignores the variable and warns
  • Fixed claude mcp add and claude mcp remove with project scope deleting other top-level keys from .mcp.json, such as $schema or another tool's servers
  • Fixed /export overwriting an existing file without asking: the dialog now asks, and /export <name> keeps the file and says to run /export
  • Fixed a command you had allowed still running after you pressed Stop, when the approval arrived after a restart, in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions with no feature flags loaded
  • Fixed Enter closing /teleport's load error screen
  • Fixed a click followed by Enter in /plugin installing or disabling a plugin
  • Fixed a half-typed ! command running on an extra Enter after the usage limit menu
  • Fixed some --disallowedTools rules with parentheses in their content
  • Fixed auto mode ignoring some wildcard PowerShell allow rules that name a script with .\, such as PowerShell(.\scripts\build.ps1 *)
  • Fixed a running Code Mode script in auto mode getting permission prompts and denials once Claude started a second script that auto mode also allowed
  • Changed some pre-started background sessions to be discarded after an account change
  • Changed a workflow paused at a usage limit in the terminal to stay paused after a login, until the earlier login returns or you type a prompt
  • Fixed a nested claude with its own token being refused by forceLoginOrgUUID: commands that don't get the session's token no longer get its CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_SCOPES; set it on any that need it
  • Fixed headless sessions losing stored messages on resume when a message was sent again with the same UUID after the process was killed
  • Fixed cases where a session resumed after an empty reply or a killed command lost an answer, or brought back a rewound prompt, after another crash or a move to the background
  • Fixed a remote session forgetting messages sent after Stop was pressed during a restart, if Claude Code then crashed
  • Fixed tasks created after /clear being lost, and cleared tasks coming back, when a cloud or self-hosted runner session with no feature flags loaded resumed later
  • Fixed a compaction right after a reply cut at the output token limit losing that reply's tool call and its result
  • Fixed a settings change from /config and similar commands failing to save with no warning; a line under the prompt now says so
  • Fixed /rewind closing without a word when some files could not be restored
  • Fixed pasted images being dropped when the prompt starts with a file path such as /tmp/a.txt
  • Fixed agents passed with --agents being lost once plugins loaded or reloaded
  • Fixed a plugin's agent being dropped when resuming a session from the --resume picker
  • Fixed Claude Code refusing to start when https_proxy or HTTPS_PROXY is a bare host:port and neither its input nor its output is a terminal (the desktop app, an SDK, cron)
  • Fixed Claude Code on Linux sometimes returning to the shell while restarting itself at startup, such as after the first sign-in to a Claude apps gateway or when turning on Code Mode
  • Fixed claude -p hanging before its first request when the fetch of a model's settings stalled, such as at a proxy; it now goes on without them after 10 seconds
  • Fixed the screen staying blank or frozen after a brief out-of-memory error
  • Fixed a rare display fault that could freeze the screen or end the session
  • Fixed cloud sessions breaking when a program left thousands of connections open to the session's network proxy
  • Fixed a turn hanging when a mod's $.model.complete or $.model.classify call met a usage limit: the call now gets the API's error at once; mods should handle that error
  • Fixed stalls on a compaction reply with thousands of unclosed tags and on some very long WebFetch URLs; WebFetch now refuses a URL over 2,000 characters before any permission prompt
  • Fixed a message with thousands of @ mentions stalling before Claude replies; only the first 100 mentions are now looked up as files
  • Fixed the prompt freezing after rejecting a write to a very large file; a rejected write now shows a short preview
  • Fixed a crash when a burst of keys reached the search box in /plugin
  • Fixed a false crash report and exit code when a suspended session resumes, or at exit, where a Linux security policy blocks a process from signalling itself
  • Fixed remote MCP servers staying disconnected after a longer outage such as a VPN drop: most servers on other machines reached by hostname over https are now retried in the background for about a day
  • Fixed Edit refusing with "File has not been read yet" after a compaction on unchanged files outside the project that Claude had already read in full
  • Fixed Grep repeating or skipping results when paging with head_limit and offset; content and count results are now sorted by file path
  • Fixed Read failing on Jupyter notebooks that contain an output of an unknown type
  • Fixed NotebookEdit removing the notebook file's final newline
  • Fixed the Read tool reporting 512KB instead of the real size when a file of 10 MB or more is too large to read at once
  • Fixed the Bash tool's diff of changed files not naming files that are binary, too large or too many to show
  • Fixed artifact publishes failing with "the source file changed between approval and publish" when a synced or remote-backed folder had only changed the file's timestamp
  • Fixed a new artifact that you approved being refused in a cloud scheduled task's session, in organizations that require approval of each new artifact
  • Fixed a new artifact being refused after an app built on the Agent SDK approved it, in organizations that require approval of each new artifact
  • Fixed /artifacts showing part of your list, or "No artifacts yet", when a request for more of the list failed: it now tries again, then warns if it can't load the whole list
  • Fixed in-process agent teammates on a different model from the lead compacting at the lead's context limit and on the wrong model; they now use their own limit and model, at that model's rate
  • Fixed a finished subagent resuming on the model and effort of a sibling subagent that messaged it
  • Fixed the main conversation not being told a background agent had finished when the subagent that started it ended by itself without reading the result, outside auto mode
  • Fixed Claude reporting a background agent as still running when it had waited 30 seconds or more on a permission prompt in the desktop app, on the web and in the SDK
  • Fixed Claude not being told in auto mode when a background agent's reply to a follow-up message was dropped, and reduced repeat wake-ups there from agents waiting on background commands
  • Fixed the desktop app, Claude Code on the web and VS Code showing a raw task notification as a subagent's prompt after its background task woke it
  • Fixed messages sent from another session with "later" priority joining the running turn, instead of waiting for it to end, in Remote Control and Claude Desktop sessions
  • Fixed messages to cloud and Remote Control sessions being reported as failed with a stale address after a timeout or rate limit; Claude now says when a message may have arrived
  • Fixed cloud sessions giving no error when a UserPromptSubmit hook blocks a message sent while Claude works
  • Fixed failing hooks showing nothing: SubagentStop in background agents, SessionEnd at /clear and /resume, and CwdChanged and FileChanged in fullscreen
  • Fixed a Stop hook that failed to run being shown as having reported a problem
  • Fixed focus view keeping a finished reply hidden while a Stop hook was running
  • Fixed Claude getting a long managed PostToolUse hook output twice when a mod added context to the tool call
  • Fixed /model listing the wrong models in some terminal sessions when a project's .claude/settings.json sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to an LLM gateway
  • Fixed /statusline writing to ~/.claude/settings.json when CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR points to another folder
  • Fixed claudeMdExcludes patterns on Windows not matching a path whose drive letter is written in the other case
  • Fixed claude agents and claude rm refusing to remove a fully pushed session ("The worktree has unpushed commits") when its worktree has a file or folder named HEAD at the top level
  • Fixed long ListAgents results hiding most sessions on accounts with many cloud or Remote Control sessions: long lists now come in pages
  • Fixed slow turns in resumed sessions for organizations with tens of thousands of connector tool permissions
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed claude -p started by a session's script or hook waiting out rate limits, because it inherited the session's own retry setting
  • Fixed the spend limit menu reporting a changed limit when the server refused it
  • Fixed a second x on a task's details in /tasks stopping the next task too
  • Fixed Esc being ignored on a permission prompt that had just appeared
  • Fixed lists that load their rows late sometimes ignoring Enter and the arrow keys
  • Fixed /autofix-pr holding the keyboard after Esc while it stopped the cloud session; the dialog now closes at once, and a stop that fails is reported afterwards with a link
  • Fixed a blank screen and stray mouse codes in the shell after quitting with ctrl+c just after ← opens the agents view
  • Fixed Ctrl+C right after the trust question leaving the terminal in fullscreen
  • Fixed the shell flashing on screen when ← opens the agents view in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed terminal display faults: most scrambled scrollback in Ghostty on resize, link addresses hidden in Windows Terminal under old tmux and in VTE 0.50.0, and no selection highlight with 16 colors
  • Fixed some garbled rows in tmux with allow-passthrough on inside kitty, Ghostty or iTerm2
  • Fixed /mcp saying no servers were configured after one was added during a session or declined; it now says what to do
  • Fixed /hooks leaving out hooks given by --settings
  • Fixed the / menu listing a row for each skill of the same name, though every row ran the first
  • Fixed /teleport showing no message when the chosen session failed to resume
  • Fixed n and N in transcript search skipping matches
  • Fixed cancelling a transcript search (ctrl+o, then /) in a long session landing far from where the search started
  • Fixed up and down losing the cursor's column over a short or blank line
  • Fixed Tab in shell mode filling in a file name after &&, ; or |, where a command goes
  • Fixed the selected session leaving the screen in claude --resume and /resume when branch names or folder paths are long
  • Fixed the MCP tool list in /mcp and /plugin losing your place when going back from a tool
  • Fixed /resume listing one session fewer than the window has room for, and a 'Resend your message' hint after most spend caps, where resending can't help
  • Fixed an MCP server's long question being cut off after one row, text fields hiding long pastes with no sign, and a doubled divider line in /plugin's options and /login's Bedrock and Vertex steps
  • Fixed the "+N lines" count being too high for command output with links or colors, and the transcript's ? help hiding how to exit in a short window
  • Fixed Ctrl+C twice not closing /chrome from its browser list
  • Fixed a number and Enter typed too early at an agent's plan approval in screen reader mode causing the next number to be dropped too
  • Fixed Claude trying to read design system token files that do not exist when starting a deck or design
  • Fixed exit not saying that a worktree was kept
  • Fixed /hooks help naming input fields that do not exist
  • Fixed question dialogs naming ctrl+g after the external editor key was rebound
  • Fixed two sign-in error messages that pointed to the Claude subscription option on computers where forceLoginMethod is set to console
  • Fixed /config saying the dialog was dismissed instead of "Set theme to …" after changing the theme
  • Bug fixes and reliability improvements
  • Improved the speed of a session's first Bash command: shell start-up files may now run before it's approved, even if it's refused; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_SHELL_HEAD_START=1 to turn this off
  • Improved commits on newer models and in PowerShell: Claude is now told not to commit files that likely contain secrets
  • Improved sandboxed shell commands: Claude now sees when a command exempt from the sandbox stayed in it because its permission check relied on the sandbox
  • Improved the refusal for shell commands with no rm that the dangerous rm check can't parse, so Claude can resend harmless ones in plain syntax instead of giving up
  • Improved resuming very long sessions: a transcript read that ends early is now retried once, so messages are lost less often
  • Improved subagent answers that hit the output token limit twice: they now more often come back whole or say up front that they are partial
  • Improved long replies on unrecognized models: a reply cut at 32,000 output tokens now continues with a limit of 128,000
  • Improved the reminder about a completed subagent after compaction: if Claude can't read the agent's output file, it is now told to ask the agent with SendMessage
  • Improved the warning shown when an API key and an Anthropic profile are both set: it now says which one is in use and how to switch to the profile
  • Improved /plugin: the question before removing a marketplace now says that its plugins' settings and saved data are deleted, and a marketplace's page no longer shows another marketplace's error
  • Windows: Improved start-up time with no Git Bash and no pwsh on PATH by checking PowerShell's standard install locations at once; System32's powershell.exe now wins over one earlier on PATH
  • Improved startup time on Windows when PATH points to Git for Windows' bin folder, by starting git.exe directly instead of through its launcher
  • Windows: Improved PowerShell tool speed by up to about half a second per command
  • Improved how soon the Bash tool's diff of changed files is ready in auto and bypass permissions modes
  • Improved speed of the Bash permission check on very deeply nested missing paths on macOS and Linux, and of secret masking on very long text with a URL
  • Improved transcript search to find text in edits and written files
  • Improved speed of reading large PNG images, and the quality of the JPEG sent in their place
  • Improved the Artifact tool to read an uploaded file by the address the artifact's page shows; other forms still fail, most with a message that says to read uploads one per call, by id
  • Improved the Artifact tool to ignore prompt, limit and label on some calls that do not use them instead of failing the call
  • Improved MCP server pages in /mcp: local, remote and agent servers share one layout, menus end in Back, and actions are no longer numbered outside screen reader mode; use the arrow keys and Enter
  • Improved narrow terminals: /status, forms and detail screens lay out better, /model and /effort fit at about 40 columns, and key hints such as ←/→ to adjust stay
  • Improved /install-github-app: the repository, secret and API key steps use the standard list and keys, with shorter messages, a spinner and clearer errors
  • Improved /desktop: the download question is a standard list instead of y/n
  • Changed ExitWorktree to ask before removing a worktree that may hold unsaved work; refused in don't-ask mode or with nobody to answer, unless an allow rule, auto or bypass permissions mode allows it
  • Changed claude mcp add --scope project to stop, instead of overwriting the file, when .mcp.json lists its servers at the top level with no mcpServers key
  • Changed the arrow keys on most permission prompts to stop at No instead of wrapping around; a number past the last answer moves to No
  • Changed path checks to refuse some symbolic links
  • Changed what counts as inside a working directory, so some paths now ask for permission
  • Changed permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories to ask about more Bash commands in bypass and auto modes, and to deny some in auto mode
  • Changed permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories to refuse more Bash commands that name a path under a Read or Edit deny rule, where it used to ask
  • Changed auto mode's notice about falling back to billed classifier requests to say that an upcoming release removes the fallback; each action it would have checked will be asked about or denied
  • Changed auto mode to ignore more allow rules that run any package, like Bash(pnpm dlx *), and path or version forms of ones it already ignored (/usr/bin/npm run:*); the safety check decides those
  • Changed /sandbox and most /config value lists to be unnumbered outside screen reader mode; use the arrow keys and Enter
  • Changed Bash commands whose variables expand to very long text to be denied, with a message that says to use shorter values or a file
  • Changed the PowerShell tool to ask before one more command, even under a rule naming it; if nothing answers, it's refused unless a whole-tool rule, auto mode or bypass permissions mode allows it
  • Changed a subagent resumed by a sibling's message to follow the session's permission settings; it may now ask, or be refused where nobody can answer
  • Changed --worktree with a relative --add-dir beside the launch folder to give the Bash sandbox that folder, not one beside the worktree
  • Changed some --worktree starts with a relative --add-dir above the launch folder, such as .., to give the Bash sandbox, and a --bg session, only the worktree
  • Changed Claude in Chrome to refuse uploading some credential files; attach those to the page yourself
  • Changed artifact approval in organizations that require it for each new artifact: an artifact that only a plugin created or allowed can be refused
  • Changed sessions with nobody to ask to refuse a new artifact at once, with no permission prompt, in organizations that require approval of each one
  • Changed the Artifact tool to refuse calls once settings turn Artifacts off, in sessions already running too
  • Changed the Artifact publish prompt to stop offering "don't ask again" in subagents and after a background task result, someone else's message or a compaction
  • Changed claude plugin eval to keep its deny rules over a plugin's permission hook, and to flag calls the hook let through
  • Changed MCP server logs to record the mode, action, and field names of elicitation requests and hook answers, not their full contents
  • Changed most prompts to ignore answers other than Esc for a moment after resuming with fg
  • Changed Code Mode to no longer refuse to start when an installed mod hooks tool calls; an administrator can still keep Code Mode off in managed settings
  • Changed subagents launched without a model to stay on the model they started on when resumed, including after /model
  • Changed the first subagent on a model to wait up to 1.5 seconds (10 in claude -p) for that model's settings from Anthropic, instead of starting without them
  • Changed restarted background subagents, and turns that start by themselves, to wait for plugins to load
  • Changed prompt history to leave out most launch prompts of sessions that another Claude Code session started, such as claude --bg run by Claude
  • Changed subagent progress summaries in terminal sessions on Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and Microsoft Foundry to be written from short notes, not the whole conversation, using far fewer tokens
  • Changed non-interactive (-p) mode to run fewer git commands before the first request
  • Changed first-run setup to skip terminal setup in remote VS Code, Cursor and Devin Desktop sessions, where it cannot change settings
  • Changed fullscreen text selection to leave out the glyph of system, thinking and inbound message lines
  • Changed Anthropic-hosted cloud sessions to ignore more of a repository's flag and plugin delivery settings; its CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC now acts at most as DISABLE_TELEMETRY
  • [VSCode] Added "Claude Code: Add to Chat" to the Explorer's right-click menu, which @-mentions the selected files and folders in the chat
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt not showing the reason that a PreToolUse hook gives when it asks for confirmation (#85950)
  • [VSCode] Fixed long tool and file names being cut off in a permission prompt's title
  • [VSCode] Fixed a terminal session's diff showing the previous proposed edit after you typed in it and Claude edited the same file again
  • [VSCode] Fixed Escape also stopping Claude's response when it closes the feedback or "Build a custom style" dialog, the @-mention menu, the model, mode or "+" menu, or another popup
  • [VSCode] Improved speed when Claude makes several edits in a row: queued edits share one wait for new problems; a problem may be reported with a later edit
  • [VSCode] Improved @-mention file search speed in large workspaces when rg is on your PATH; results now rank much as in the terminal, with less tolerance for typos
  • [VSCode] Improved startup: the model picker is ready at once in folders opened for the first time, empty windows and worktrees, except on third-party providers
  • [VSCode] Changed a chat edit's diff to stay open and keep asking for approval when a terminal session in the same window sends a prompt
  • [VSCode] Removed unused tools from the IDE connection (openFile, saveDocument, getOpenEditors and related)

items.title: Meta’s Muse: Inside the launch of the most successful consumer product this year | Mona Sarantakos
items.summary:
Muse is the #1 app in the App Store and arguably the fastest-growing AI consumer product of all time. Mona Sarantakos has led product on it since day one. She’s VP of Product at Meta Superintelligence Labs and a 10-year Meta veteran with over 20 years of experience as a PM. This is her first podcast interview.

*We discuss:*
1. How a weekend with OpenClaw on a Raspberry Pi turned into Muse
2. Why Muse waited seven months to launch, despite getting started before most of its competitors
3. How Nat Friedman, Alex Wang, and Mark Zuckerberg each left their imprint on the product
4. How the team uses “agent swarms” to surface user insights at scale
5. The use case nobody on the team predicted
6. How Jolly, a placeholder avatar, became an icon
7. The two levers that actually move activation for an AI agent
8. The #1 thing Mona looks for in PMs today

*Brought to you by:* 
WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more: https://workos.com/lenny
DX—Engineering intelligence for the AI era: https://getdx.com/?utm_source=lenny&utm_medium=sponsorship&utm_campaign=q42026

*Episode transcript:* https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/metas-muse-how-we-launched-the-most
*Archive of all Lenny's Podcast transcripts:* https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fo/yxi4s2w998p1gvtpu4193/AMdNPR8AOw0lMklwtnC0TrQ?rlkey=j06x0nipoti519e0xgm23zsn9&st=ahz0fj11&dl=0
*Highlights:* https://lennyspodcast.com/mostreplayedmoments

*Where to find Mona Sarantakos:*
• LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/mona-sarantakos-a85873
• Threads: https://www.threads.com/@monachaudhuri

*Where to find Lenny:*
• Newsletter: https://www.lennysnewsletter.com
• X: https://twitter.com/lennysan
• LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/lennyrachitsky/

*In this episode, we cover:*
(00:00) Teaser

(02:14) A weekend with an early agentic AI
(09:08) The seven-month launch timeline

items.title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
